paragraphs.text: Chapter 3. Stress Control

I, like everyone else, don’t like the feeling of being stressed, but I have grown accustomed to the idea that life inevitably involves stress. Whether it was my high school classmates (most of whom were very driven), the athletes I’ve met, or the students, professors, and people in tech or creative fields around me, I have always found that stress accompanies ambition, and that for many of the top achievers, it’s a constant.

The weird thing is that many of the unambitious people I have known often said they were stressed out too. Lack of direction, lack of money, the feeling they were slipping behind in life, health issues, and more… Eventually I had to conclude that this was indeed part of life—like breathing, sleeping, or eating. That meant there had to be a good way to address it.

The problem was that when I looked to see what the science said about stress, it was uniformly negative. It made clear that stress wasn’t just uncomfortable, it was damaging to the brain and body. And that only made stress more stressful. Moreover, the whole framing of stress seemed wrong, or at least rather one-sided.

For instance, “fight or flight” is one of the most common phrases we hear when the topic of stress comes up. It’s easy to remember and it seems science-y—because it sounds like it could describe how the brain and body respond to stress. Unfortunately, it’s more misleading than informative. We also often hear that the stress response is an inconvenient holdover from our evolutionary past. Meaning, the uncomfortable state of arousal we call stress was helpful for us long ago, propelling us to escape from saber-toothed tigers and other large predators, but it’s no longer useful.

I always appreciate when science shows up in a conversation, but I confess phrases like “fight or flight” make me shake my head. It’s not just that they are misleading; they also don’t provide any valuable information about how to navigate the stress response. And actually, the stress response is no holdover. And research has shown that the beliefs we hold about stress can change how stress impacts our health, for better or for worse, so we need to be careful what we tell ourselves about it. [^1]

Stress is an area I’ve thought a lot about from a neuroscience perspective. My lab has studied it in animals and humans. Decades into my career, I now know that there is, in fact, a good way to address it. There are excellent stress management tools based in science. So, given how pervasive stress is, I am especially excited to share the information in this chapter.

First let’s begin with the facts. Forget saber-toothed tigers. Many of the same situations that stress us out now have been stressing out humans for thousands of years. An argument with a loved one, a persistent pain of unknown cause, a worry about a child, a looming payment, and on and on. Scenarios like these are not unique to modern times.

A good way to think about stress is this: Stress is nature’s attempt to create a single solution to all matters that might be, or actually are, urgent. I’ll say that again. Stress is nature’s attempt to create a single solution to all matters that might be, or actually are, urgent.

So no matter what the stressor (and there are an infinite number of them out there), the basic architecture of the stress response—that is, what happens to our brain and body when we perceive a stressor—is the same. Cortisol and other hormones, including the catecholamine neuromodulators adrenaline and norepinephrine, flood our system. Adrenaline, or epinephrine, as well as cortisol are released from our adrenal glands. Norepinephrine is released from specific locations in the brain including the locus coeruleus, which we discussed in chapter 1 and chapter 2. Dopamine is released in the brain and in the body too. All of these chemicals change the activity level of specific neuronal circuits and, in doing so, initiate a coordinated shift in the ways our organs function, and thus in our overall state of mind and body. We often hear about the increase in heart rate, breathing, and blood pressure that stress brings about. Less discussed, however, are the perceptual changes. Stress changes our visual field and narrows our mental attention. [^2] We become fixated on the events related to the stressor: “How did this happen? How can I undo this?!” Stress causes our perception of time to slow down. Seconds start to feel like minutes, minutes like hours, hours like days… Meanwhile, our rate of thinking—the sheer number of thoughts we have per second—seems to speed up. And yet, our cognitive flexibility is reduced. We default to simple black-and-white thinking. Nuance evaporates. Mild-to-moderate stress makes us feel jittery whereas intense stress can cause us to freeze. At its extreme, it can make people feel as if they have left their body, as if they are viewing themselves from above. [^3]

While that all sounds dreadful, we must remember that the stress response is adaptive. The purpose of it is to put our brain and body into a state that gives us the best chance of addressing the problem at hand. A single solution. In an ideal world, the degree of stress response would perfectly match the stressor we face. Running late? A little bit more arousal to help us focus on the key items we need to get out the door with grace would be perfect. See our toddler running toward the traffic? A huge surge in energy to quickly grab them is what we want! In fact, the parts of our nervous system that govern stress—called the autonomic nervous system—can be calibrated to generally match our stress level to the stressor we face, from mild to severe, from brief to ongoing. [^4] But nowadays, the many comforts most people enjoy thanks to technology—indoor heating and air conditioning, abundant food and shelter, and all in all our general lack of actual survival stressors—have our autonomic nervous systems uncalibrated. We are far more labile under the constant barrage of minor psychological stressors all day and night, and a lot of people are in a constant state of stress related to things they simply cannot control or influence even slightly. Put simply, the frequency and/or magnitude of the stress response is far too high relative to the stressors many people face. The occasional bout of stress lasting a few hours or less is no big deal, and even a few days is something our bodies can handle without long-term consequences. Once we experience a few weeks to a month or more of daily (which usually also means nightly) stress, that’s when we start to suffer. Chronically elevated resting blood pressure and heart rate, not sleeping well or enough due to rumination or feeling “tired but wired,” and other shifts to our internal state become detrimental to our immediate and long-term health. We’ve all heard the laundry list of things that stress harms: our hormones, memory, mood, and decision-making ability, as well as the many diseases it makes worse or can bring about to our heart, brain, gut, and liver. The body of evidence that chronic stress is bad for us is vast and robust.

Yet some stress is good for us. In fact, the occasional spike in our stress hormones can increase testosterone [^5] and improve our immune system functioning during the hours that follow. [^6] In the short term, it can improve our memory. [^7] The problems arise when the intensity or the duration of the stress response is too great.

Eliminating stress from our lives is unrealistic. So our goal with stress should be twofold. First, we need to be able to adjust the intensity and the duration of our stress response so we can better handle stress in the moment. Second, many of us need to increase our stress threshold—that is, the subjective point at which events and thoughts trigger large amounts of adrenaline release in our body—so our stress response is calibrated to any stressors we may encounter. Ahem, I mean, that we will encounter. When adrenaline release occurs as the consequence of tiny things, that is not good. It negatively affects our physical health and relationships, including our relationship with ourselves. Do you like being around you when you’re stressed? Didn’t think so. We can change our relationship to stress through cognitive reframing, but an effective approach is to learn to quickly control our stress response once it hits, and to periodically reset our stress threshold to a level that best serves us. We can’t always control what life throws at us, but we can indeed control our stress response, and we can raise our stress threshold. That’s what this chapter is all about.

I first became interested in investigating the neuroscientific mechanisms behind stress back in 2015. At the time, grit, resilience, and mental toughness were popular themes in books and media. And those are great qualities. The examples—both historical and contemporary—of people being gritty and resilient and mentally tough are there to remind us that humans harbor within them an enormous capacity to manage and even channel their stress.

While there is a lot known about the neural circuits and hormones that control the stress response, I specifically wanted to understand the mechanisms that determine its intensity and duration. I wanted to know which features of the stress response, like heart rate, blood pressure, attentional narrowing, and so on, were amenable to adjustment in real time. I also wanted to know whether there are levers for adjusting the duration, the intensity, and maybe even the probability of the stress response getting triggered in the first place.

I was able to find some data about stress inoculation, [^8] including some studies supporting the idea that certain forms of early-life stress can set the stage for resilience later in life by virtue of how they tune the physiology of the stress response to better match the intensity of a stressor. [^9] But it was hard to find evidence for specific tools that kids or adults could reliably apply to recalibrate the stress response across different circumstances. I wanted to find mechanistic data that could be translated broadly and that were accessible for the average person.

I continued my search. I found studies on the benefits of positive self-talk [^10] but just as many studies on its lack of effectiveness. [^11] Despite the fact that we are all born with the same biological stuff—adrenals that release adrenaline, locus coeruleus neurons that release norepinephrine, and prefrontal cortices that can exert top-down control over our impulses and feeling states—I just couldn’t find any really convincing studies in humans that pointed to tools people could use to improve their capacity to manage stress. Meanwhile, we know that slogans like “Just do it” and mantras like “Embrace the suck,” or telling ourselves “You got this,” can be good for pushing us through a stressor we have chosen to face—a long run, the final reps of a hard set in the gym, a study session or big exam—but most people would agree that self-talk fails the vast majority of the time when the stressor isn’t one we’ve chosen, or when our efforts have us falling short of our goals. And at some point, real life brings the sorts of stressors we simply cannot control, like a medical emergency or the loss of a beloved friend or family member. In those circumstances, “Just do it” just doesn’t do it.

Of course, much has been researched and written about what I call offline practices to manage stress. Meditation, massages, vacations, hot baths, deep breaths, talk therapy. Great! Who doesn’t love a massage at the end of a hard day? Meditation is powerful as a tool to buffer against the stress response; a randomized clinical trial conducted by researchers at Georgetown University found that people with generalized anxiety disorder who meditated experienced a noteworthy reduction in pro-inflammatory cytokines—chemical messengers essential to our immune system but that can also trigger a stress response—compared to those who didn’t meditate. [^12] Other studies, including one done by my lab at Stanford in collaboration with my colleague David Spiegel’s lab, also at Stanford, have shown clear benefits of meditation practices as short as five minutes per day on stress, mood, and sleep. [^13] That might seem like a trivial level of time commitment, especially given the many benefits of meditation. [^14]

But I wanted to know how people can navigate stress while they are in the throes of the stress response. When their pulse is racing, their vision is blurry, their hands are shaking, and all they can think about is the stressor and the potential bad outcomes from it. That’s when the capacity to manage stress matters most. Not offline, but in the moment.

As I pointed out above, the stress response is universal. Whatever the specific stressor might be, the stress response is the same. It varies in degree, not kind. This suggests that if we have reliable tools to reduce the stress response in one context, we ought to be able to reduce it in another. The problem? No one had dissected the universal features of stress control, only the stress response.

One valuable thing everyone should know about the stress response, though, is that it is asymmetric: It starts extremely fast and turns off relatively slowly. The adrenaline release that is the first domino of the stress response happens in seconds or less and can continue for several minutes after we perceive a stressor. [^15] Think of a time when you were groggy from just waking up and you picked up your phone to see a disturbing text. BOOM! You are wide awake and ready to move in an instant. That’s the speed of adrenaline in action.

Then, even after the stressor is resolved, the stress response persists. Imagine getting a text that says, “I think Mom was on the flight that just crashed,” and ten minutes later, “I just spoke to her, she wasn’t on there. She’s fine.” Your feeling of relief will no doubt outpace how quickly your body settles down. That’s an extreme example, but the same thing applies when someone almost sideswipes you while driving, and you swerve just in time to avoid a collision. A shot of adrenaline wicks out through your body in an instant, and almost as fast, norepinephrine is released to ramp up attentional circuits in your brain. Cognitively, you realize you’re safe almost as quickly as you thought you were about to get hit, but your body and mind don’t relax immediately. More often than not, we plummet into the stress response and it takes time to return to baseline. And that’s when everything turns out okay. When stressors persist, you experience wave after wave of adrenaline. And while the basic circuits for stress are the same in everyone, seldom discussed is that not everyone has the same threshold, or trigger point, for a stress response to kick off. For some people it’s as if that first domino is fixed in cement. Such people are rare. For most people, however, the domino falls too easily. I wanted to understand this aspect of stress too, in order to develop tools anyone can use to raise their stress threshold, to allow them to calibrate their autonomic set point. That is, the balance point that our nervous system works to maintain—so that the stress response happens when it’s needed and not when it isn’t. Even better would be to find ways such that when stress does happen, it occurs in proportion to the stressor. I wanted these tools to be mechanistic and behavioral, not pharmacological, because pharmacological tools—while they can be helpful—don’t allow for real-time adjustments. You swallow a pill and that’s that. And they have to be taken before stress arrives, which is problematic because we don’t always know when stressors are coming. I also wanted to develop tools that do not rely on practice, like cognitive behavioral therapy, which is great but can take a fair amount of time to master [^16] and doesn’t always translate across stressors very well; there is evidence both for and against generalizability. [^17] Like all protocols in this book, I wanted tools for stress management that could be effective the first time and every time because they are anchored in hardwired circuits and processes we all possess. So I dove into the research on the physiology of stress to come up with a different way to frame the whole concept of stress. And stress control. That led to…
The Seesaw Model

Think about the stress response as existing somewhere along a spectrum of arousal, with very low arousal at one end of the spectrum and very high arousal at the other. At the extremely low arousal end is a comatose state. Slightly more aroused than that would be deep sleep, then light sleep. Then toward the middle of the spectrum is a state in which we are alert but calm (which incidentally is the ideal state for most of our waking activities). As we progress further along toward the highest arousal end of the spectrum, we enter mild stress, then severe stress, and finally, full-blown panic. When we think about stress on a spectrum of low-to-high arousal, we realize that arousal—and what increases or decreases arousal—is the thing to focus on if we wish to deliberately lessen the stress response.

Where we happen to be on the spectrum of arousal at any given moment reflects the level of activity in our autonomic nervous system. Our autonomic nervous system regulates involuntary functions like our heart rate, digestion, blood pressure, and breathing. It also controls our level of alertness, and thus our ability to focus. It is comprised of two sets (sometimes called “arms”) of neural circuits: the parasympathetic nervous system (PNS) and the sympathetic nervous system (SNS). These function more or less independently of one another, but their balance of activities combines to determine our arousal level, and thus our overall brain and bodily state. [^18]

But what sets the balance between these two systems? Or, to put it another way, what regulates our autonomic nervous system? There are three main categories of autonomic regulators. The first is our twenty-four-hour circadian rhythm. [^19] If you follow a typical diurnal schedule—awake in the daytime and asleep for a major portion of the night—then your SNS activity levels will dominate in the daylight hours and your PNS will dominate at night. In fact, the incredible impact your circadian rhythm has on your ability to reason, [^20] exert physical effort, [^21] and resist infections [^22] stems from how it controls the balance of SNS versus PNS activity. In the morning and early daytime, elevated SNS activity (sometimes called “sympathetic tone”) caused by a natural and healthy increase in our baseline levels of cortisol makes us physically stronger and better able to focus, whereas in the later evening and at night, when our baseline cortisol levels are markedly lower, our parasympathetic tone is elevated, and we become mentally and physically weaker, and our immune system becomes far less capable of warding off infections. [^23] (Circadian variation in the expression of specific genes and the actions of various molecules—neuromodulators, hormones, peptides, etc.—are what underlie those dramatic morning-versus-nighttime variations in autonomic tone, as discussed in chapter 1.)

The second category of things that control our autonomic nervous system, and thus our level of arousal, are the sensory inputs—or stimuli, as neuroscientists call them—that we experience. For example, our level of physical comfort or pain, how well-fed or hungry we happen to be (not surprisingly, hunger makes us more alert), whether we are in a brightly lit or dim environment, the environment is quiet or loud, et cetera. And, of course, by the presence or absence of psychological stressors. In general, when we are hungry, thirsty, tired, or otherwise in need of basic sustenance, our arousal levels increase and, with that, our propensity to think and move increases. It should be obvious why that is adaptive. (It helps us seek out food, water, etc.)

The third category of things that control our autonomic nervous system is pharmacologic. Caffeine and other stimulants are sympathomimetic, meaning they stimulate the SNS and increase arousal. [^24] Other drugs promote PNS activation, and thus decrease arousal levels. For example, alcohol and barbiturates indirectly increase PNS circuit activity, [^25] as does the molecule apigenin, which is found in chamomile tea. [^26] By the way, if you’re wondering why alcohol initially makes people more talkative and alert before it makes them drowsy or has them pass out, it’s because before it reduces central nervous system activity and lowers arousal, alcohol first transiently stimulates the SNS. “It lifts you up before it drops you,” as they say.

Autonomic means “automatic” and indeed our sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems are, for the most part, not under our direct conscious control. We of course can adjust them indirectly. We just discussed three categories of ways to do that. The pathways and mechanisms by which different activities like exercise, [^27] or mechanical inputs like massage or a warm bath, [^28] or drugs like caffeine [^29] elevate or lower arousal by adjusting the activity of our SNS or PNS are fairly well known, but again, it’s crucial to note these are all indirect ways of adjusting autonomic arousal. As such, they tend to be slow and hard to titrate—meaning hard to get just right. Moreover, some, like barbiturates or prescription stimulants, have addictive potential and/or are costly.

There is, however, one major exception to all of this: one lever by which we can quickly, directly, and reliably change our level of autonomic arousal by shifting the balance of SNS versus PNS activity. That lever is our respiration pattern, aka our breathing.

Why? Because the neural circuits that control our breathing are part of our autonomic nervous system. In fact, they are the one (and only!) component of it that is both autonomic—breathing works just fine without us having to think about it—but that we can also consciously and directly control at any moment we choose. The same cannot be said about our heart rate, digestion, or immune system. As my colleague at Stanford, David Spiegel, MD, has described it to me, breathing and the neural centers that control breathing represent a bridge between our conscious and unconscious mind. We will return to this idea shortly, but to understand the specific patterns of breathing that allow us to consciously and directly control our stress response, and to understand the best tools for adjusting our stress threshold, we need to take the autonomic spectrum—that continuum spanning from deep states of calm to intense states of panic I described earlier—and turn it into a seesaw.

A seesaw? Correct. The simplest model for understanding how to control stress is a seesaw: parasympathetic at one end and sympathetic at the other. When the seesaw is tilted toward the parasympathetic end, we feel calm and relaxed. Tilt it further in that direction and we start drifting off to sleep. A flat, balanced seesaw represents when we are alert, but calm. Tilt it a bit in the other direction, toward the sympathetic end, and we feel more alert and energized. Tilt it further, and we feel stressed. At its steepest tilt, we are in full-blown panic. Reducing the intensity or duration of the stress response can be accomplished either by increasing the load on the parasympathetic side, by reducing the load on the sympathetic side, or both. How do you do that? We just need to understand a bit about the neural circuits and physiology of the SNS and PNS. And how breathing impacts each of these.

Because it turns out that inhales and exhales modulate the activity of our autonomic nervous system. Inhales reduce PNS activity, leading to relatively more SNS activity and thus, arousal. Exhales directly increase PNS activity. This means your heart rate is faster during inhales than during exhales—which incidentally is the basis of heart rate variability (HRV). Higher HRV in sleep and throughout your day is better than lower HRV, because it means PNS activity is periodically slowing your heart rate down. It’s a good marker of your body controlling its own level of arousal, and keeping stress in check. [^30] More on all that later but for now, it’s going to be helpful to understand what “feeling stressed” is about at a neurochemical level. If you are stressed, that likely means that adrenaline and cortisol have been released and are circulating in your body at higher-than-typical levels, and that norepinephrine has been released at higher-than-typical levels. [^31] You can’t just make those molecules go away with positive self-talk. Also, when stress hits, your prefrontal cortex changes its pattern of electrical firing in a way that limits the range of solutions you can come up with to a problem. [^32] It even changes your ability to link previous experiences in insightful ways. [^33] Most of us are familiar with this stress-induced black-and-white thinking. These facts should help alleviate some of the frustration you may experience when someone tells you to “just relax,” and you can’t. Or when someone says, “Don’t worry, this too shall pass.” The first form of encouragement ignores that we must actively do something to our physiology to relax. You can’t out-think adrenaline. The latter encouragement is spot on, as stress does indeed hinder our ability to see the big picture, but it’s not particularly helpful in the moment. It’s sort of like telling you that the splitting headache you’re suffering from right now won’t suck in the future. Fortunately, there is a way to get right to the physiology of the stress response. Rather than try to directly reduce sympathetic tone, you need to instead tilt the seesaw back toward the parasympathetic side by increasing the activity of your PNS. That is going to be the fastest way to calm down in real time whenever you are feeling stressed.
Resilience defined

If you think about it, this is a big part of what resilience is really about. It’s not our ability to tolerate or eliminate the stress response but rather our ability to reduce its intensity quickly and in real time, when our arousal exceeds a useful level, so that we can move forward. Resilience is our ability to control stress. Sometimes that means going from extreme stress to very alert and energized, so we can perform a task and quickly problem-solve under intense pressure. Other times it means taking ourselves from endlessly looping thoughts to deep sleep. Resilience is also about an ability to deliberately increase our stress threshold, so life’s minor stressors don’t disproportionally hijack our mind and body. Once you learn how to do those two things, then you will truly be in the driver’s seat.

Maybe that all sounds overly simplistic. Easy to say but harder to do. Well, it turns out there are science-supported tools to adjust your stress response in real time and to raise your stress threshold, and they work exceedingly well—and fast. They can also work the first time, and every time, because they are grounded in biological mechanisms and circuits that you already have inside you and can access. Some involve adopting a specific pattern of breathing, but they are not breathwork. After all, when we find ourselves in a high stress situation, we can’t run off and do five minutes of box breathing! Other protocols don’t involve breathing at all. I’ve been blessed to play a partial role in the discovery and application of several of these stress control protocols, although like so many other scientific “discoveries,” aspects of them were known about and used by nonscientists in other contexts first. None of us gets the patent. The following pages explain what they are, how they work, and how to use them.
STRESS CONTROL PROTOCOL 1 Do One to Three Physiological Sighs to Reduce Stress Fast
WHAT TO DO

• Breathe in the pattern known as the physiological sigh. Inhale deeply through your nose until your lungs are full (your belly should expand out while you inhale), then sharply inhale a second time, also through your nose, to maximally inflate your lungs. Then slowly exhale through your mouth until your lungs are empty of air. Repeat this in-in-out breathing pattern up to three times, in succession, as needed to reduce your stress level (meaning, your level of autonomic arousal) fast.
HOW IT WORKS
Physiological sighs are, to my knowledge, the fastest and most effective way there is to deliberately calm yourself down. Often just one physiological sigh does the trick.

That’s because our state of mind and body changes our breathing but our breathing also changes our state of mind and body. [^34] Remember the locus coeruleus that releases norepinephrine to make us alert? Well, specific populations of neurons involved in specific patterns of breathing connect directly to and modulate this release from the locus coeruleus. [^35]

The conversation between the neurons in your brainstem that control breathing also extends downward, into your spinal cord, which contains neurons that in turn control the muscles between your ribs (called the intercostals) and a dome-shaped muscle attached to the bottom of your rib cage called the diaphragm that actively inflates and deflates your lungs. [^36]

When we inhale, oxygen enters our body, fills our lungs, then passes from our lungs into our bloodstream. That only happens because our lungs are not just two big, hollow bags; they contain hundreds of millions of tiny sacs called alveoli, which inflate with air as we inhale. The walls of the alveoli are extremely thin—about 1/2000th of a millimeter (!)—and yet rich with capillaries, the smallest diameter blood vessels. Together, they allow oxygen to move from the air-filled alveoli into the bloodstream. Having hundreds of millions of alveoli greatly increases the surface area through which oxygen can pass into our blood, and thus increases the amount of oxygen we absorb with each breath. (As wild as it sounds, you have approximately 70 to 100 square meters—about the size of a regulation tennis court—of alveolar surface area packed inside your lungs.) Big, deep breaths inflate more alveoli and the more alveoli that inflate, the more oxygen passes into your bloodstream to get delivered to your organs, including your brain. [^37]

Carbon dioxide from the bloodstream passes into the alveoli—again through capillaries—and then is expelled from your body when you exhale. We need both oxygen and carbon dioxide, but we need them in the right balance. If we breathe too little, carbon dioxide builds up in our brain and bloodstream, leading to headaches and tiredness. [^38] If we breathe too much—rapidly inhaling and exhaling, or what we typically call hyperventilation—we expel too much carbon dioxide, which is problematic because carbon dioxide is crucial for making sure oxygen gets to our brain cells. If you’ve ever wondered why it’s advised to breathe into a paper bag if you’re having a panic attack, it’s to recapture some of the carbon dioxide that would otherwise be expelled. In this chapter you’ll learn faster and better ways to calm down, but the logic is the same. Overbreathing causes anxiety, dizziness, confusion, poor sleep, and even muscle spasms. [^39]

As mentioned in the introduction to this chapter, the neurons in our brainstem that control our breathing represent a bridge between our conscious and unconscious mind. They are equipped to sense the ratio of oxygen to carbon dioxide in our blood, which prompts any necessary alterations in our breathing pattern to keep us alive and well. That happens regardless of whether we are exercising hard or deeply relaxed—it even happens while we sleep. [^40] Unlike other autonomic neural circuitry, however, we can take immediate conscious control of these neurons. We can decide “I’m going to extend my next exhale a bit” or “I’m going to take one more inhale before holding my breath” and—voila!—we can make that happen. We just don’t have that level of conscious control over any other autonomic function. There are some reported examples of people who used biofeedback to learn to directly control their heart rate or the size of the pupils of their eyes, but that requires a fair amount of training. [^41] Extended exhales and physiological sighs are something that anyone can do.

Certain internal states are associated with certain respiratory patterns. And by deliberately changing how we breathe, we can shift our internal state. That’s a big deal and something I wish they had taught us in grade school. Alas, it wasn’t until recently that Western science embraced controlled studies of respiration and, in doing so, revealed what had been known in Eastern traditions for thousands of years. We owe it to a small set of dedicated researchers, mostly neuroscientist Jack Feldman’s lab at UCLA, for discovering how the brain controls breathing, both our unconscious reflexive breathing and deliberate breathing, and how they impact our emotional and cognitive states. [^42] Before and during our discussion on the Huberman Lab podcast, Jack told me stories of setting out to study this topic in the early 2000s, and a luminary of neuroscience making fun of him at meetings. He would jab: “Why would you study something as boring as breathing? Why don’t you study something important, like memory?” [^43] (That guy studied memory.) Jack knew to ignore him and follow his intuition. His work ignited a field that is now positively impacting the mental and physical health of people of all ages. Detecting and modifying certain breathing patterns also turns out to be important for predicting heart attacks, [^44] strokes, [^45] and seizures, [^46] and for preventing sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS). [^47] Some of his recent work has also shed light on the fact that some opioid drugs can lead to death because of how they change the firing patterns of the neurons that control breathing. [^48] It is fair to say that Jack’s work has literally saved lives.

Breathing isn’t just about getting oxygen into your lungs; it also helps control heart rate. While you can’t directly control your heart rate, you can leverage the fact above and use your breathing to control it indirectly. Deliberately inhaling more vigorously or longer (or both) increases your heart rate, whereas deliberately exhaling more vigorously or for longer slows your heart rate down, through a process called respiratory sinus arrhythmia. Exhales also activate a specific branch of the vagus nerve, which is part of the PNS, which in turn reduces the rate of electrical activity in neurons of the sinoatrial node of the heart, your heart’s natural pacemaker. So deliberately emphasizing the intensity and/or duration of your exhales for a few breathing cycles will caaaaalm youuuu dooooown. The breathing pattern described in this protocol does just that.

Once you learn the relationship between breathing and heart rate, and deploy the physiological sigh to reduce your heart rate on the spot, it gives you a significant feeling of confidence in dealing with stress, and uncertain circumstances too. You no longer have to be afraid you will get stuck in an anxiety response in a key moment, or any moment for that matter. You also realize that what most people say to themselves or others when stress hits—“Take a deep breath”—is the exact opposite of what we need to do! When stress hits we should do a big exhale. It is when we really draw out that exhale that our heart rate starts to slow down.

So why am I recommending “Do one to three physiological sighs to calm down fast” and not just “Do a big exhale”? And why aren’t I suggesting box breathing, a popular breathing pattern that asks you to inhale-hold-exhale-hold, each in equal duration? Because some breathing techniques are far more potent and fast acting than others for stress reduction. And physiological sighs are particularly powerful for that purpose, because they capitalize on a hardwired set of neural circuits and neuromuscular pathways, which at once slow our heart rate down and adjust our oxygen–to–carbon-dioxide ratio in our brain and our bloodstream. The first two steps of the physiological sigh—the long inhale, followed by the quick inhale—are vital because of those hundreds of millions of alveoli we discussed. The insides of alveoli are a bit damp, not unlike a deflated balloon that once held water. And they tend to stick together due to surface tension. The long inhale inflates many alveoli, and the second quick inhale that immediately follows helps generate the force needed to reinflate alveoli that would otherwise stay deflated. This is especially effective when you inhale through your nose, because nasal breathing generates more resistance than mouth breathing and thus more force to reinflate those alveoli. Doing a physiological sigh also stimulates a collateral (meaning a branch of a neural pathway) that emerges from the brainstem area controlling your breathing and reaches other brain areas important for emotional and cognitive control. [^49] Thus, physiological sighs, unlike just a big exhale or box breathing, are a three-pronged tool to quickly (1) slow your heart rate, (2) reestablish proper oxygen–to–carbon–dioxide ratios in your brain and bloodstream, and (3) engage brain areas that let you think logically about your situation. It’s adaptive biological engineering at its best and works to calm you down.

Infants do physiological sighs reflexively. [^50] Animals do too. [^51] Observe a dog right before it goes down for a nap. You’ll see that double inhale, long exhale pattern. Rats physiological sigh when placed into a claustrophobic environment. [^52] People reflexively do physiological sighs about once every few minutes when working [^53] and even in their sleep to reset their oxygen–to–carbon-dioxide ratio. [^54]

In fact, you have dedicated sets of neurons in your brainstem for generating physiological sighs. [^55] Nature just doesn’t create discrete neural pathways by accident; that’s how important this breathing pattern is. One respiratory region, the pre-Bötzinger complex, controls your rhythmic breathing, the regular alternation of inhales and exhales. [^56] But a second region, the parafacial nucleus, controls breathing that involves double inhales, double exhales, or any combination of inhales and exhales in ratios other than the 1:1 inhale-exhale pattern. [^57] The parafacial nucleus does things other than generate physiological sighs but that’s one of its primary functions.

I’d like to clarify that physiological sighs are not breathwork. Breathwork refers to setting aside five to twenty minutes to do a specific breathing pattern (or designated sequence of patterns) to get you into a specific state of mind and body. Physiological sighs are a naturally occurring breathing cycle that we can deliberately recreate. And they are the fastest way to consciously tilt your seesaw to the parasympathetic side of your autonomic nervous system.

Do it before public speaking or a hard conversation. Do it when you’re stuck in traffic or late to an important meeting and starting to feel your tension level rise. Do it to stop yourself from overreacting to an offhand comment. It won’t guarantee that you’ll always do the right thing in response, but it will put you in a better frame of body and mind, so that you have the best chance of navigating the stress that comes from these or similar situations.

There are data showing that doing physiological sighs outside of stressful moments can help buffer you against future stress too. [^58] Several years ago, my lab collaborated with psychiatrist David Spiegel to investigate just that. [^59] We conducted a study that randomized 108 participants to one of four groups. One group did five minutes per day of cyclic physiological sighing: Inhale, inhale, long exhale, repeat, and so on for five minutes. The second group did five minutes per day of box breathing, a breathing technique I’ve mentioned before, which follows a pattern of inhale-hold-exhale-hold-repeat, where each inhalation and exhalation, and the holds, are the same duration, until five minutes have elapsed. The third group did five minutes per day of cyclic hyperventilation: You take a big deep breath in through the nose and a shorter exhale through the mouth, putting more vigor into the inhalation than the exhalation. A fourth group did five minutes per day of meditation, seated with eyes closed, and focusing their attention on their breath but with no specific instructions about breathing pattern.

Most participants, regardless of their group, reported an improvement in mood and outlook. But cyclic physiological sighing had a notably bigger effect. We also observed improvements in resting heart rate, improved sleep, and other metrics of well-being related to autonomic function. In other words, doing one to three physiological sighs is a great tool for when stress hits and doing five minutes of physiological sighs on repeat can help buffer us further against the inevitable stress of life. Given what you now know about exhales slowing heart rate, oxygen and carbon dioxide levels, and the autonomic seesaw, it should make sense as to why this works. Your brain and body were literally built to do this.
STRESS CONTROL PROTOCOL 2 Use Deliberate Cold Exposure to Raise Your Stress Threshold
WHAT TO DO

• Put yourself in uncomfortably cold water three to seven times per week. This can be as simple as a cold shower, or as involved as an ice bath. For the duration, choose one of these options: Timed protocol: One to three minutes per session.

• Count “walls of adrenaline” protocol: Rather than committing to a specific amount of time, try committing to a specific number of mental “walls” to climb over. When you feel the impulse to avoid or exit the cold but you stay, that’s one wall you’ve scaled. Decide in advance how many times you will encounter this impulse and keep going. You do not have to always increase the number of walls. There are days when you will decide to “go over” five walls and other days where two walls will be enough.

• The water should be uncomfortably cold. This means it should immediately trigger your impulse to get out, but it should be warm enough that you can safely stay in the water for up to three minutes. Why do I suggest using such annoyingly subjective criteria? Because the specifics will differ by person, the time of day, the ambient temperature, how well rested you are, and on and on. It should be cold enough to require you to overcome some mental resistance to get in. And once you get in, it should be cold enough to cause your breathing to quicken. It should make you want to raise your shoulders. If the water is so cold that it burns or gives you a headache, however, it’s probably too cold. For most people, somewhere between 40 and 50 degrees Fahrenheit works great.
HOW IT WORKS
The previous protocol will help reduce the intensity and the duration of your stress response. This one takes a different approach to stress control by increasing your stress threshold.

But let’s first address some of the common myths about deliberate cold exposure. You may have heard that it can increase your metabolism. In my view, the data are not strong enough to support those claims, at least not by doing a typical one-to-three-minute cold shower or cold immersion (and staying in the cold much longer than that could be unsafe).

You also may have heard to avoid deliberate cold exposure after any resistance training session aimed at increasing muscle growth and/or strength. That counsel is legitimate. Deliberate cold exposure in the six to eight hours after resistance training can prevent some of the strength and hypertrophy adaptations that would otherwise occur. (Chapter 2 explains more about those adaptations, and how to achieve them.) That inhibition of muscle growth is likely due to the vasoconstriction the cold causes, which limits both nutrient delivery and waste removal from the recently trained muscles and also blunts protein synthesis. [^60] Wait at least six hours after resistance training to do deliberate cold exposure, or do it before you train, or just save it for another day. Or do it any time relative to your resistance training, but be sure to end with a hot shower or bath to reestablish perfusion of the muscles to correct for this. One study argued that deliberate cold exposure done in the first six hours after resistance training does not prevent strength adaptations, but most of the work on this issue indicates that deliberate cold exposure done in the six hours or so after resistance training will significantly reduce any hypertrophy or strength increases that would otherwise occur. [^61] So it is best to simply do it before resistance training, or on rest days. Or allow six or more hours to elapse after resistance training before deliberate cold exposure.

Another common myth is that deliberate cold exposure is harmful for people wishing to limit their cortisol levels. You often hear that people should avoid deliberate cold exposure to keep their cortisol levels low too. Yet the cortisol increases caused by deliberate cold exposure, while significant, are transient and small compared to the dramatic increase that a moderate intensity exercise session triggers. [^62] You won’t hear that people should avoid exercise to keep cortisol low because the cortisol increase caused by exercise is, again, transient and, what’s more, beneficial. (Indeed, it is a key aspect of the specific and general adaptation triggers we discussed in chapter 2).

Many of the “cold exposure is bad for you” stories involve people going into the cold for very long periods of time at excruciatingly cold temperatures, or combining deliberate cold exposure with hyperventilation breathwork and/or jumping or diving under ice. All of which are dangerous and should be avoided.

Now that those points are out of the way, let’s look at why deliberate cold exposure is beneficial. Done correctly, deliberate cold exposure is a powerful, safe, and reliable tool for rapidly adjusting your internal state and stress threshold. There are two key phases, each with distinct benefits. First, the state shift that occurs during the cold exposure itself. Second, the state shift that occurs for many hours afterward. Anyone who has done deliberate cold exposure consistently—that is, three to seven times per week—will tell you there is a third phase too, which is the change in your subjective experience of stress and your ability to navigate other forms of stress.

When you enter the cold, it sharply tilts your autonomic nervous system toward the sympathetic end of the seesaw. It does this the first time and every time, and it happens fast, within one to two seconds upon entering the cold. Then, once you get out of the cold, you tend to remain in a very “alert but calm” state—meaning (in the context of the model I described) with an evenly balanced autonomic seesaw—for many hours afterward.

Deliberate cold exposure increases the levels of circulating catecholamines in your brain and body: adrenaline, norepinephrine, and dopamine, and increases in the hormone cortisol too. [^63] Some, including dopamine in particular, remain elevated long after you dry off and warm up. [^64] These catecholamines increase mood, energy, and alertness. They also can increase your stress threshold; more on that below. [^65] But first I want to pause for a moment because you may be asking this: Why would I want to trigger the release of these “stress” chemicals? Won’t that make me feel more, not less, stressed? Yes, but that’s what this protocol is all about.
We need to challenge the notion that stress is always bad for us.

In fact, when we have control over when, how much, and especially for what purpose we experience stress, the impact of that stress can switch from being health-perturbing to health-promoting, and this reshapes the body’s response to all forms of stress. [^66] This is not “mind over matter,” it’s leveraging the brain circuits that convert the arousal response we call stress into something called eustress—a term coined by Swiss physiologist Hans Selye. [^67] (You may remember him from the previous chapter.) He was nominated for the Nobel Prize seventeen times for his work on this and related topics, [^68] long before we knew what the underlying mechanisms were, but as those mechanisms have become elucidated, many of his theories have largely been deemed correct.

We now know that your prefrontal cortex—that patch of brain real estate involved in context-dependent decision-making (as well as “top-down” inhibition of impulsive actions) is also a key component of our limbic system, which is involved in different arousal-based responses. [^69] Usually when people talk about the limbic system, they focus on the amygdala, a brain structure often touted as our fear center. They also talk about our reptilian brain, which is pop neuroscience language for structures like our hypothalamus, which contains dozens of subareas involved in regulating hunger, thirst, aggression, mating, and much more. The hypothalamus and amygdala are often placed conceptually opposite “more evolved” or “higher” brain centers like the prefrontal cortex. But alas, that framework is a gross misrepresentation of the way our brain actually works.

Human brains don’t have one system for positive arousal and another entirely different system for negative arousal. We simply have a system for autonomic arousal that is linked to, and impacted by, areas of the brain that evaluate the context of our experiences and then help us make adaptive decisions. Think about it: There are an infinite number of different contexts in which arousal could be good, and just as many where it could be bad. Your prefrontal cortex carries out the basic analysis when arousal happens, asking questions like, “Did I choose this situation?” “Can I control how long and/or how intense this arousal is?” and most importantly, “Is this state of elevated autonomic arousal good or bad for me?” Of course, the answers to those questions depend on the context. And your prior experiences and knowledge.

In fact, our knowledge about stress—not just our memories of stressful circumstances we have been in before, but what we believe to be true about stress—affects how we respond to it. Work from Alia Crum’s lab at Stanford shows that humans who learn about some of the (true) positive effects of stress-related arousal on physical health and mental performance experience those positive effects when they are subjected to stress. [^70] Her lab also showed that if people learn a bunch of (also true) information about how stress can make us physically unhealthy and cognitively impaired, well, that’s what happens to them when they get stressed! [^71] We can thank our prefrontal cortex for that ability to reframe stress in ways that change its actual effects on us. It’s not just a decrease in its negative effect but an inversion from deleterious to beneficial. There’s more that shapes our experience of stress as good or bad. Perhaps one of the most interesting things that determines the outcome is whether the stressor has a known end point and resolution that we control. [^72] With that in mind, it should now make perfect sense why deliberate cold exposure meets all the criteria of eustress, and why I coined it deliberate. If you are the one who elected it, and you control its duration, and you understand how it is good for you, you can turn stress into eustress.

So how, exactly, is it good for you? Two ways. First, the stress of deliberate cold exposure helps us become better at handling other moments of stress. That’s sometimes called cross adaptation. It’s often studied in the context of physical stress, where exposure to one type of stress—say, exercising in extreme heat—prepares a person to tolerate another type of stress, such as thriving in environments with low oxygen levels. [^73] The idea is that we can precondition ourselves to cope with challenges by seeking out situations that draw on similar aspects of our physiology. Cold water swimming has been proposed as a way to improve surgical outcomes, [^74] for example, because the stress of the former helps patients better handle the stress of the latter.

Controlled studies showing that cross adaptation focused on physical stress can prepare us to face emotional stress are slowly accruing. In one study of eighty-six people, combining cold exposure with breathing techniques changed the participants’ perception of stress in their everyday lives. [^75] Participants rated statements such as “You feel calm” and “You enjoy yourself” following a few minutes of vigorous breathwork and a quick cold shower every morning for a period of two weeks. And participants who did both during that period reported a greater sense of control over irritations, and stronger feelings that life was going their way and that they were on top of things, compared to participants who did only the breathwork or the cold exposure, or neither.

Some data are more tangential in nature. For example, cold exposure appears to improve the body’s response over time to hypoxia, or low oxygen levels in the blood, which is relevant because hypoxia can rapidly set in when we hit a state of anxiety or panic. [^76] Some preliminary evidence has pointed to a possible role for cold exposure in the treatment of depression, not as a replacement for medication but as an accompaniment. [^77] In 2018, a group of researchers from the UK reported that a twenty-four-year-old woman who had been treated for major depressive disorder and anxiety since the age of seventeen with little to no relief began weekly sessions of cold water swimming in an attempt to find something that could diminish, or negate, the need for medication after she became a mother. The intervention worked for her. Within four months, she no longer required drug treatment. [^78] That was a case study of just one person, but interesting nonetheless.

A 2023 review of fourteen studies on the mental health benefits of outdoor cold-water swimming found this practice to be associated with stress reduction, mood improvement, and a positive outlook. [^79] That result is not necessarily entirely tied to cold; being outdoors and part of a community (many people do winter swims in groups or with friends) certainly contributes, but cold exposure is responsible for at least some of this benefit. Other work has also shown a connection between winter swimming and well-being. [^80] In one study, fifty-three people in the UK who participated in eight weekly sea swims reported a reduction in both depression and anxiety. [^81] Interestingly, “confronting a challenge” was commonly reported as a reason why the experience was rewarding. In another investigation, forty-two undergraduates at the University of Chichester, in the UK, completed a mood profile questionnaire before and after cold immersion, with an additional twenty-two students completing the questionnaire twice but without cold immersion in between. [^82] Energy and self-esteem increased significantly in the experimental group, which also experienced a decrease in tension, anger, and depression. No comparable changes were observed in the control group.

The overarching concept here is really about the intentional discomfort brought about from doing deliberate cold exposure. As Mike Tipton, a sports and exercise scientist who has studied cold exposure extensively at the University of Portsmouth, has noted, the kind of discomfort stemming from a cold bath was once a commonplace occurrence. [^83] Humans have been exposed to cold for a very long time, and modern living has eliminated it. As a result, we are never forced to move out of homeostasis, which means our various systems are rarely challenged. “The dynamic equilibrium that underpins homeostasis needs to be perturbed,” Tipton wrote in an editorial first published in 2018. Stanford University psychiatrist Anna Lembke, author of Dopamine Nation, has also spoken about the role of deliberate pain exposure to combat addictions. As she explained it, we are living in the midst of a “fire hose of dopamine,” triggered by our phones, caffeine, sugar, and other aspects of modern life. [^84] And part of the way out of this is to temporarily abstain from pleasure and to intentionally seek pain—not life-threatening pain, not anything dangerous, but discomfort. [^85] We need to learn to cope with stress, not just eliminate it. Stress is a part of life, and we are capable of withstanding it. Cold immersion shows us how.

The second way deliberate cold exposure is good for us is the state it puts us in after it’s over. And no, I’m not just talking about a state of relief—although it is fair to say that nearly everyone enjoys getting out of the cold plunge or cold shower more than getting into it. In all seriousness, very few people actually enjoy deliberate cold exposure while they are in the cold. It is a potent stressor and no amount of learning about eustress will change that. In fact, I often find myself cursing Selye when I’m in the cold. But once we get out, ahhh, that’s when the real magic starts. The sharp increase in adrenaline, norepinephrine, and cortisol we just triggered also sets in motion a dramatic and prolonged increase in dopamine—the molecule that, as we will discuss more in chapter 6, induces a heightened sense of motivation and focus and, with the pain of the cold now gone, buzz. Dopamine doesn’t act alone to create the post-deliberate-cold state, but it is a central player in that neuroendocrine cocktail. It’s the perfect state for a work session, for exercising, socializing, pretty much any activity that requires us to be alert and focused.

If the way I’m describing the post-cold state sounds almost drug-like, it is. Only better. One study found that full-body (up to the neck) immersion in water at about 57 degrees Fahrenheit for one hour triggered a more than fivefold increase in norepinephrine levels compared to baseline. [^86] It also produced a rise in dopamine levels in the body, raising them more than twofold for hours afterward. We call this peripheral dopamine, because it was measured from the body. We don’t yet know the exact relationship between dopamine levels in the body and in the brain, but we do know they tend to increase and decrease in parallel. And there is emerging evidence that when peripheral dopamine is elevated, it increases dopamine in reward and motivation circuits in the brain in a dose-dependent manner. [^87] When adrenaline is released in the body, it doesn’t cross the blood-brain barrier but it does activate receptors in the vagus nerve that project from the body to the brain. In doing so, it causes the locus coeruleus to release norepinephrine, which increases alertness in the brain. So there is reason to assume that peripheral increases in catecholamines triggered by deliberate cold exposure are mirrored by similar increases in the brain.

It is worth noting that drugs known to sharply increase dopamine and epinephrine, such as amphetamines or cocaine, also produce fast, large increases in catecholamines but with the important caveat that they cause levels of the catecholamines to rise so fast and then drop so fast, that they plummet below pre-drug levels. That is part of what, as Anna Lembke, MD, explained in Dopamine Nation, puts people in a state of psychological and physical discomfort, and leaves them craving more of those drugs right away, which partially explains why they are addictive. [^88]

Deliberate cold exposure then seems an almost perfect way to significantly increase and maintain elevated levels of catecholamines. You get the mental focus and mood benefits they provide, and you also raise your stress threshold.

Most of us don’t have an hour available to spend sitting in chilly water, however. Fortunately, you can use colder temperatures for much shorter periods of time to get the same effect. Studies show that even thirty seconds can work. [^89] Yet I suggest one to three minutes or two to ten “walls.” As mentioned above, pinpointing an exact temperature for every reader isn’t possible because it will vary according to differences in the amount of body fat, time of day, tolerance for cold, and other factors. That being said, adrenaline levels reliably increase when we expose our body surface to temperatures below 59 degrees Fahrenheit (15°C) and the colder the water, the faster and larger the resulting catecholamine response will be. This relationship isn’t linear. We cannot say, “Sit in this temperature water for this long and you’ll get this much more adrenaline and dopamine released.” It doesn’t work like that. We don’t work like that. Nor can we say that x number of minutes in x degrees water will elevate our dopamine x amount for x number of hours after.

That’s why, although I refer to deliberate cold exposure as a protocol, like resistance training or cardio, you will need to consider what number of sets, so to speak, works best for you. It is best thought of as a time to practice triggering specific types of adaptations to build resilience. Some people say you should try to relax and breathe slowly during deliberate cold exposure. Others suggest distracting yourself with mental arithmetic or singing a song. I disagree and view both those approaches as the loss of a valuable opportunity to focus on stress control. You can take this time to learn to steer your mind and body through the stress response.

Resilience, grit, and mental toughness are really about the ability to stay in control of your thoughts, words, and actions when you experience that stress response. When you get into the cold, your prefrontal cortex experiences a surge in norepinephrine input, which causes a disruption in its communication with subcortical areas. [^90] This is true of any stressful circumstance, whether deliberate or involuntary. With your prefrontal cortex function essentially impaired for the first thirty seconds after you get in the cold, all your thoughts and actions initially will default to removing the stressor. It’s where the immediate “I want out!” response comes from. The key is to remind yourself that it is normal to feel like that. You’re in what I call “pure impulse” mode. Do this: Try to consciously watch your mind shift from “I want out!” to “I’ve got this,” which will likely happen again and again very rapidly in that first thirty or so seconds. By observing that phase and not trying to grind your way through it, you are actively engaging your prefrontal cortex in a way that is not typical of someone going through a mild cold-shock response. That’s an extremely valuable skill, to be able to observe your own mind during stress. It’s not about passively observing or dissociating, nor is it about getting hijacked by stress. It’s about learning adaptive self-control during stressful moments.

The first time you try this, it’s hard, but most people find that within a few sessions the mind racing starts to lessen, and pretty soon, they feel in control of their thoughts and actions from the start. Few people have mastered this valuable skill in any domain of life, but anyone can learn it. Deliberate cold provides a safe way to practice.

I believe the walls approach mentioned above is the best way to practice this skill, whose benefits translate to other forms of stress. When we measure time elapsed in the cold, we focus, not surprisingly, on its passage. As you learned in the introduction to this chapter, high arousal states tend to slow our perception of that. We count, we wonder why time seems to be moving so slowly—a known function of stress—and we focus on it… 3, 2, 1, okay, done! Real-life stressors are very different. Some hit when we least expect it (e.g., an accident or crisis), others are stressful in large part because we know they are coming (e.g., a public talk we need to give, a medical appointment we would sooner avoid, etc.). The way to train for real-life stress in the cold is therefore to learn to sense the increases in adrenaline that occur as we approach, enter, stay in, and exit it. Each of these can be the walls you need to climb over. If you think like that, you’ll notice something very useful: Stress is not constant. It’s not, as we say, a step function. It oscillates, often very quickly and irregularly. The walls appear, and then disappear and reappear with unpredictable frequency.

If you dread the cold, remember that adrenaline is released merely from the anticipation of getting in. Congratulations! That’s the first wall. And as we lower ourselves into the cold, that’s another wall; next comes the first “I want out!” wall, then it passes… then comes the next wall, the next, and the next. Importantly, the time between walls is variable. This is also important to notice, as that is exactly how real-life stress feels. We often can’t predict when the next stressful event is coming.

Basically I’m suggesting you approach deliberate cold exposure as resilience training. And by doing it you’ll become mentally stronger in the face of nonvoluntary stress. Just be sure you don’t stay in the cold longer than five minutes. Stick to the one to three minutes recommended here, or “go over” two to eight walls. Then get out and go about the rest of your day. Some people, myself included, like to take a hot shower after deliberate cold exposure. People debate whether it’s better to end on cold or not. I don’t care. I like a hot shower after and, in my experience, it does not seem to diminish any of the benefits. Find what works for you.

As a final point, you actually have more moment-to-moment control over the temperature of the water than you may think. While you can’t quickly make the water temperature change, you can dynamically adjust your experience of it. If you hug your arms around your body, raise your shoulders toward your ears and bring your knees up toward your chest, you will feel slightly warmer. Conversely if you keep your arms and legs extended and move them around, you’ll break up the thermal layer of heated water around your body, making the experience much colder. Want it even colder? Make sure to let the cold water reach as high as your armpits and keep your hands and feet under. You’ll want to remind yourself that this is all very good for you now, and in the hours to come. Cursing Selye, as I do, or cursing me (feel free), is allowed and encouraged.
COMMON QUESTIONS
Is deliberate cold exposure safe

Cold exposure can be dangerous if the water is exceedingly cold. Exercise caution and prudence with this tool. If you are new to cold immersion, start off slowly, with short exposures in temperatures that are outside your comfort zone but not extremely so. Try a cold shower, which allows you to adjust the temperature higher or lower quickly. Alas, there is not much data on deliberate cold exposure for pregnant women so if you’re concerned about potential negative outcomes, avoid this. Don’t do it when sick with a cold, the flu, or other respiratory illnesses. Regardless of what you may see online, it’s likely to make your illness worse. Here’s a good set of guidelines for nonpregnant individuals with no serious health issues:

• Start with water around 50 degrees Fahrenheit the first time, maybe in the mid- to high 40s. Test the water temperature with your hand or foot before getting in; it should feel cold and make you think, “Whoa, that’s cold!” but it should not “burn.”
• If the water triggers a reflex to raise your shoulders and huddle your arms when you get in, then it’s cold enough. If your breathing involuntarily quickens, it’s cold enough.
• Get in up to your neck with your feet under. Put your hands under last.
• If you opt for a cold shower, back into the water until your whole body and head are underneath the stream.
• Expect your mind to start racing with thoughts like, “I want out! Why am I doing this?!” Congratulations, you have a functional autonomic nervous system.

Note: Never, ever jump or dive into very cold water. Lower yourself in while holding something reliably stationary like a ladder or the sides of a cold plunge, or back into a cold shower. I recommend against deliberate cold exposure in cold or frozen outdoor bodies of water unless you have an expert with you, know the location well, and there are real safety measures in place. There is a video on the internet of a woman who drowned after jumping into an ice hole; unbeknownst to her, there was a rapid current under the ice and she was swept under. Her husband allegedly went in after her and also drowned. I have a professor friend who nearly drowned doing deliberate cold exposure in a river. He had done at-home cold plunges many times before but hadn’t realized how cold the river was until he swam out a few feet from shore. He couldn’t breathe properly in a shocked state and he was alone. Have someone with you and decide on a nonverbal signal for “Save me!” before you get in.

Never—never, ever!—combine immersion in cold water with any type of deliberate hyperventilation before or during. Your breathing will naturally quicken when you get in cold water, but what I am referring to is deliberate hyperventilation (Wim Hof or Tummo breathing, as it is sometimes called). This breathing method causes the lowering of carbon dioxide and will delay the gasp reflex, potentially leading you to black out and drown; sadly, people have died this way.
Deliberate cold exposure is easy to do safely. Almost all deaths from it occur because people were reckless in some way or combined it with hyperventilation. Don’t be reckless.
Are there additional benefits to deliberate cold exposure

A study from metabolic scientist Susanna Søberg, at the University of Copenhagen, and colleagues showed that if people did eleven minutes total per week of deliberate cold exposure, divided into two to four sessions, they enhanced the amount of brown fat in their bodies, a healthy, mitochondria-rich fat that surrounds the heart, neck, and clavicles. [^91] That additional brown fat allowed them to feel more comfortable in other cold environments, because when the sympathetic nervous system is active it causes brown fat to burn fatty acids and glucose, which generates heat in the process. In that way, brown fat is like an internal furnace. So if you’re someone who is often cold, deliberate cold exposure can help shift your thermal set point. This is connected to the metabolic benefits of cold immersion, which are outside the scope of this protocol. (Note that the participants didn’t gain weight; they just added this special—and beneficial—type of fat.)
I hate the cold so much. Is there any alternative method

Yes. As an alternative to deliberate cold exposure, you can do three to five minutes of cyclic hyperventilation away from water, which reliably raises adrenaline levels. Cyclic hyperventilation, as the name suggests, involves taking long, vigorous inhales through your nose and passively exhaling through your mouth—think of it as letting the air fall out rather than forcing it out—over and over. It’s not easy to keep up this breathing for several minutes. You’ll find it makes you quite agitated and a bit lightheaded.

Data suggest that cyclic hyperventilation works similarly to cold exposure. [^92] Adrenaline rises. Your heart rate increases. Your limbs will feel like they want to move. And your brain will ask “Why am I doing this?!” It’s normal to feel some light burning in your nostrils as well. It feels uncomfortable while you’re doing it, but it can improve mood and sleep afterward. Also, you can back off the intensity and/or duration of the inhales and thereby modulate your stress response as you go, an advantage that cold exposure doesn’t offer.

So if you really hate the cold or if you don’t have access to it, cyclic hyperventilation is the next-best alternative. Just never do it in combination with deliberate cold exposure as, again, you can pass out and drown. People have died combining cyclic hyperventilation with cold immersion; that’s why I’m repeating the warning here yet again. And of course never do cyclic hyperventilation while driving or operating machinery, or other activities that demand your attention. Just sit or lie down somewhere safe for a few minutes to use this tool.
STRESS CONTROL PROTOCOL 3 Do Non-Sleep Deep Rest (NSDR) to Buffer Against Stress
WHAT TO DO

• Do a non-sleep deep rest (NSDR) session for 10 to 30 minutes. Sit or, ideally, lie down in a quiet place and listen to a scripted NSDR session. Guided NSDRs in different voices are available online (hubermanlab.com/nsdr) for zero cost and can be downloaded to use offline (also at no cost). NSDR is especially useful in high-stress times lasting weeks or longer, such as intense work or school periods, or when facing deadlines and life transitions, such as raising young kids or caring for an elder. Ideally you do NSDR once per day but it is beneficial to reduce stress at any point. I do it at least once a week, depending on my schedule.
HOW IT WORKS

I talked about NSDR earlier in this book (remember Sleep Protocol 8?). It is impossible to overstate what an extraordinarily potent tool NSDR can be for mental and physical health. In chapter 1, I covered NSDR’s ability to restore mental and physical energy without creating sleep inertia grogginess. But it is particularly potent when it comes to limiting unhealthy stress. I was first introduced to this tool nearly ten years ago. I often get asked “What is something you wish you had known when you were younger?” and my answer is always, “I wish I had known about yoga nidra (aka NSDR).”

NSDR has so many benefits. It replenishes your mental and physical energy, [^93] it can offset many of the negative effects of sleep deprivation, [^94] it improves the depth and continuity of your sleep at night, [^95] and it buffers you against the harmful effects of both acute and chronic stress. [^96] To get the most out of this practice, I’ll make a few things clear. First, NSDR is not a nap. Nor is it hypnosis. Nor is it meditation, as I explained in chapter 1. Rather, NSDR belongs to a category of techniques that can be broadly thought of as self-directed relaxation. You shift your brain and bodily state from one of “alert and ready to move” to “alert yet deeply relaxed.” It emphasizes parasympathetic nervous system (PNS) activity, or increases your parasympathetic tone, tilting you toward that calmer side of the autonomic seesaw that I described in the introduction to this chapter. Sounds like a shallow nap… but it’s not. Because you deliberately stay awake during this practice, your sympathetic nervous system remains engaged too. It’s a unique brain state that has important implications.

Research shows that during NSDR, parts of your brain enter sleeplike states, while other brain areas remain in a state of alertness. [^97] We don’t quite know what to call the overall brain state that NSDR creates, but we know that it’s self-directed and has significant stress-reducing and energy-replenishing effects. [^98] We also know that people typically emerge from NSDR in an alert-but-calm state of mind and body, that center of the seesaw. When one considers that it costs nothing but ten to thirty minutes of time, that is quite a return on investment!

As discussed in chapter 1, NSDR involves shifting one’s focus throughout the session, which for some people makes it easier than meditations that demand you anchor your focus or “clear your mind.” NSDR asks that you shift from thinking, doing, and planning, to being and feeling—I know, that sounds super New Agey. But the instruction is based in physiology, not mysticism. Here is why: Turning off our thoughts is really hard. In fact, we can’t do it. Even in sleep, we dream. Even in REM sleep people can solve and respond to math problems. [^99] (If you’re wondering how the experimenters knew that, given people are paralyzed during REM, the subjects signaled correct answers to simple subtraction problems using eye movements.) So forget trying to destress by not thinking. It just won’t happen.

We can, however, easily shift our immediate experience from planning and analyzing to just experiencing physical sensations. NSDR has us do that. We deliberately shift our attention from one aspect of our sensations in that moment—for instance from our toes to our fingers, then to a location away from our body such as to sounds in the room, then to sounds far away, then back to a specific location on our body, and so forth. This regular and deliberate shifting of our focus on different aspects of our perception both eliminates the strain of trying to continually focus on one thing, and the tendency of our mind to default to planning and analyzing. With NSDR, your mind drifts from one sensation to the next in an intentional but relaxed way. When you do that, your mind goes into an atypical, almost liminal state, the one described above—somewhere between that of deep sleep and being awake. Cortisol levels drop, discrete brain areas fall asleep while others remain active. [^100] Because NSDR is done lying down with eyes closed, from the outside it appears you are napping but you’re not. You’re in self-directed reset mode.

If you’ve never done yoga nidra or NSDR before, this may all sound a bit abstract, but it’s really very concrete. It is grounded in what we know about self-directed brain states. And it’s very easy to do. One of the biggest advantages of NSDR is that, in contrast to mindfulness meditation—which is a skill you build up gradually over time and that requires daily (or near daily) practice to maintain the positive effects—NSDR can work the first time, and every time.

You lie down, listen to the instructions, and voila! Ten to thirty minutes later you emerge feeling renewed and rested. Most everyone who tries it marvels at the immediate positive effects. It’s starting to be used in schools, by elite military operators, professional athletes, Fortune 500 CEOs, and many other men and women around the world as a tool for managing stress and even as a means to accelerate recovery from illness and injury, to offset some of the negative symptoms of menopause, sleep deprivation, trauma, and more. [^101] I encourage everyone to try it a few times and experience the benefits for themselves.
COMMON QUESTIONS
When should I do NSDR

This is the most common question I get about NSDR. You can do it ANY time. In the morning if you wake up and don’t feel fully rested and don’t have time to get another hour or more of sleep. In the afternoon instead of a nap and if you know you’ll be working harder or longer than usual that day. Before a workout if you’re feeling less-than-motivated or lacking energy. In the evening if you get home and want to destress from the day. In the middle of the night if you wake up and can’t fall back asleep. (In that case, get out of bed and do an NSDR then get back into bed; a return to sleep will arrive easier.)
The simple answer I default to whenever asked “When should I do NSDR?” is “First thing in the morning, or in the afternoon, or any time of night…” It is that versatile and that useful.
STRESS CONTROL PROTOCOL 4 Do a Micro Meditation Immediately After Waking Up
WHAT TO DO
