• Incorporate a simple, five-minute daily meditation into your routine. Any time of day can be beneficial, but doing it before getting out of bed each morning ensures you don’t have to carve out time later and may offer distinct benefits as well.

• If you feel an urgency to get out of bed before five minutes have elapsed, stay put. Contrary to how it is usually framed, meditation is one of the best forms of resilience training. So see this as an opportunity to practice resilience. This meditation is not about clearing the mind. It’s about building the capacity to sit with the stress that even micro meditation can trigger. This will help you better deal with real-life stressors once your day starts.
HOW IT WORKS

Plenty of evidence exists that mindfulness-based meditation practices buffer us against stress, and even brief daily sessions reduce anxiety. [^102] I mention both stress and anxiety here, because there’s a difference. Some say stress has an identifiable cause, or a known stressor, whereas anxiety does not. That’s a good working distinction. But the fact that meditation protects us against both highlights that each experience is based in the same thing: an elevated sympathetic tone that exceeds the demands of the stressor.
Meditation can adjust your autonomic seesaw, bringing you back to the center. But just how may surprise you.

Most everyone assumes the goal of a meditation practice is to quiet the mind and that it involves cultivating a sense of peace during the practice. In some sense that’s true. One study found that four consecutive days of a meditation practice reduced anxiety and increased mindfulness, a broad term encompassing a sense of awareness, calm, and being in the present moment. [^103] A 2019 report by New York University neuroscientist Wendy Suzuki and colleagues found that doing eight weeks of thirteen-minute daily meditation notably decreased anxiety. [^104]

But data also show that meditation can make us more resilient by allowing us to observe stress when it hits without reacting to it. When psychologist Richard Davidson—one of the world’s foremost experts on the science of meditation—appeared on my podcast, he described that his lab saw a statistically significant increase (!) in people’s anxiety levels in the first week that they started doing a regular meditation practice. [^105] Wait, what? Meditation increases anxiety? Yes. Because it can be maddening to force yourself to focus and refocus on your breathing over and over for five minutes when you wake up and you have to dive into your day. Your mind wants to shift to planning and doing. In that way, meditation can serve as a way to increase your stress threshold. Not unlike learning to stay in uncomfortably cold water.

This is as hard as it sounds, but well worth it. Regular meditation teaches us to observe, rather than act on, our autonomic arousal. It also reduces the likelihood that real-life stressors will hijack our mind. Just like Stress Control Protocol 2.

One study found that the intensity of the emotions people experienced while viewing potentially disturbing pictures was reduced when people did so from a “mindful” state, indicating that meditation promotes a kind of awareness that makes a person’s autonomic nervous system less subject to outside stimuli. [^106] Indeed, neuroimaging studies have confirmed that meditation consistently alters brain regions connected to both body awareness and mental awareness, as well as emotional regulation. [^107] The underlying mechanism appears to be connected to the production of GABA, an inhibitory neurotransmitter—meaning a chemical that generally suppresses the firing of other neurons. People with panic disorders and anxiety tend to have decreased GABA activity in particular regions of the brain. [^108] Researchers have theorized that the increased blood flow to the prefrontal cortex that seems to occur during certain types of meditation may, in turn, lead to increased GABA activity, along with improved top-down inhibition of brain areas that generate reflexive thoughts and actions, and this equates to a general sense of relaxation. [^109]

A bit more on the format of the micro meditation: stay in bed or, if you must, get up and use the bathroom first, and then set a five-minute timer, sit or lie down, and stay as still as you can while you focus on your breathing. Observe where your mind goes. If it wanders—which is completely normal by the way—redirect your focus back to your breath. Slow nasal-only inhales and exhales are best. But the most important thing is to do it, and on days when you feel stressed, do it anyway. In fact, that’s a bonus opportunity. The benefits to your ability to observe your stress rather than have it engulf you that come from a daily five-minute meditation are well worth it. And of course, if you want to do a longer meditation, go for it.

As simple as this protocol may sound, I and countless others can attest to the fact that it provides immediate benefits, and benefits that extend throughout the day. And one more thing: We don’t yet understand the science of exactly how, but it also seems to create the ability to “see” when stress is coming your way. Perhaps it sensitizes the brain circuits that respond to autonomic arousal. Perhaps it leads to better recognition of adrenaline in our body rising, or our heart rate starting to increase. After all, a five-minute meditation will gradually have you feeling more anxious as you progress from start to finish; it’s very different from getting into cold water, which causes a big spike in adrenaline right at the start. But that ability to sense approaching stress is a game changer, as it can reduce your reactivity and improve your ability to make decisions about what to do and say—and in many cases, what not to do and say—when the inevitable stressors of life appear.
STRESS CONTROL PROTOCOL 5 Boost Your Morning Cortisol and Catecholamine Peak
WHAT TO DO

• Stack three to four of the pro-cortisol and pro-catecholamine triggers below in the morning, and limit them at night. Get bright light, ideally sunlight, in your eyes for about ten minutes, as soon as possible after waking. If you wake before the sun is up, you’ll either have to wait for the sun to rise or use a 10,000 lux light for this trigger. (I cover how in detail in Sleep Protocol 1.)

• Hydrate with 16 to 32 ounces of water and consume some caffeine in the first two hours of your day. How much caffeine? 100–400 milligrams depending on your body weight and caffeine tolerance. A strong cup of coffee or yerba maté (my preferred caffeine source) has 150–200 milligrams of caffeine. Note: Chronic caffeine drinkers don’t get as much of a cortisol increase from their usual amount of caffeine as those who aren’t, but it still has a positive effect on other catecholamines for reasons covered in chapter 1. [^110]

• Exercise in the morning. If your schedule allows, do cardiovascular or resistance training within the first two to three hours of waking; the closer to waking the better. (The foundational fitness program in chapter 2 offers a sustainable weekly structure, but of course there are many others out there.) If you can’t exercise in the morning, take a brief walk, do some jumping jacks, skip rope, or do some light calisthenics, even for just five to ten minutes. While not a full-fledged workout, it will help stimulate the morning cortisol and catecholamine increase you’re after.

• Do one of the deliberate cold exposure protocols discussed in this chapter. Remember, this takes only one to three minutes, and a cold shower works too. Just do it before resistance training, ideally not after (refer to Stress Control Protocol 2). As an ALTERNATIVE to deliberate cold exposure, try cyclic hyperventilation: Do a cycle of twenty-five to thirty deep, vigorous inhales through your nose, with each inhale followed by a passive exhale—meaning just let the air fall out of your lungs via your mouth. Afterward, you’ll feel a bit lightheaded. That is a normal response. Exhale all your air and hold your breath for thirty to sixty seconds. You should no longer feel lightheaded. You can repeat this process for two to three more rounds. Note: NEVER do cyclic hyperventilation before or during deliberate cold exposure, anywhere near water, while driving, operating machinery, or performing other activities that demand your attention. You may recall from those protocols that deliberate cold exposure doesn’t spike cortisol all that much, but it does significantly increase the other catecholamines. And that is beneficial here.

• Consider occasional (once or twice per week) use of low-dose licorice root containing glycyrrhizin or consume grapefruit in the first one to three hours of your day. Both have been shown to significantly increase cortisol and the duration of cortisol action. Subjectively, they can increase feelings of morning and daytime energy and focus. Warning: Despite licorice and grapefruit sounding natural (and they are), their effects can be very potent. They can increase blood pressure and/or fluid retention at high doses, so use the minimal effective dose and, as with all supplements discussed in this book, consult your doctor first.
HOW IT WORKS

Cortisol and the catecholamines adrenaline and norepinephrine, but especially cortisol, are often thought of purely as stress chemicals. The third catecholamine—dopamine—escaped this reputation but is usually thought of (also incorrectly) as purely a pleasure chemical. And while cortisol is involved in the stress response, thinking about it as purely a stress chemical is wrong. I wish I could banner this across the sky: Cortisol Is Not a Stress Hormone!
In fact, if I could impart just one message about how to improve your health, it would be this: Strive to get your morning cortisol high (yes, high!) and your nighttime cortisol low.

The main function of cortisol is to ensure there is enough energy in the form of glucose, or blood sugar, for you to meet life’s demands. Yes, that can include overcoming stressors, but it also includes simply waking up each morning with the physical and mental energy required for work, school, family, and exercise. Cortisol causes glucose (as well as fats) to get released into the bloodstream, and it also stimulates the liver to make more glucose. [^111]

Cortisol and adrenaline play additional key roles in our body’s everyday functioning. They improve our immune system’s ability to ward off infections, they elevate our mood, they allow for our capacity to form new memories, and they increase metabolism… so just forget the idea that cortisol and adrenaline are only about stress.

A gradual rise in your cortisol levels starts three to four hours before you wake up each morning and its levels eventually hit a threshold level, at which point you wake up, open your eyes, and get out of bed. Keep in mind that cortisol doesn’t act alone to rouse you from sleep; a parallel rise in body temperature and clearance of the sleepiness-inducing molecule adenosine follows a similar schedule. Nonetheless, scientists call this rise the “cortisol awakening response” or CAR. Now that makes it sound like a medical problem of some sort, but CAR is a normal and (provided it is timed correctly) health-promoting aspect of our biology. [^112] And it helps buffer you against unhealthy stress.

Cortisol first starts to rise as a result of a signal from your SCN, your brain’s master circadian clock that we discussed in chapter 1. For most people, that rise starts somewhere around five hours into their night’s sleep and continues sharply over the subsequent two to three hours until it reaches a threshold level and bam! You wake up. Even if you use an alarm clock, you can be sure your cortisol levels were rising as you approached the start of your day. Now, once you’re awake, cortisol continues to increase until it hits its peak for that twenty-four-hour cycle. For most people, that peak occurs anywhere from 0.5 to 1.5 hours after waking up.

Then cortisol levels slowly start to decline—a process that continues into the late afternoon and evening. Assuming you encounter no major stressors, your cortisol levels continue to drop in the hours before you fall asleep and reach their lowest level about three to four hours after you doze off, and then slowly start to rise again to eventually trigger the next morning’s CAR, and so on. This is the ideal cortisol pattern for mental and physical health, energy, and resilience to stress.

Night shift workers deal with a very disrupted sleep-wake schedule, and their cortisol pattern gets fragmented, with multiple peaks and troughs throughout the day. For some, the pattern inverts to match their wake-sleep schedule. Although that might seem like not that big of a deal if they are still getting enough sleep, it’s known to cause serious and long-lasting health issues. Indeed, many of the known health detriments of nocturnal schedules are due primarily to alterations in the pattern of cortisol release and its downstream effects. I cover what shift workers can do to partially offset those negative effects in chapter 1 and chapter 5. [^113]

Most people, even night owls or those staying up too late on their phones, are not completely inverting their sleep-wake schedule, and yet there is reason to believe that they have less than ideal cortisol patterns. I say “most people” because the vast majority of questions I get are about wanting better sleep, more energy, improved focus, and less stress and anxiety. And when I inquire about the structure of their days, I learn that very few people are doing the few simple things to ensure high cortisol in the morning and low cortisol at night. This sets them up for health problems and lowered resilience to stress.

Numerous studies show that if your cortisol levels fall too slowly as you approach the later hours of your day—a so-called “flattening of the diurnal cortisol rhythm”—or if your cortisol is spiked by stress or bright light in the evening, you can experience that as increased anxiety, and sleep can suffer too. [^114] If this happens once in a while, it’s no big deal. Acute stressors—an argument, a small crisis at work, and so on—are part of life. They spike our cortisol and catecholamines. But these levels ordinarily return to baseline a few minutes or hours later. So don’t freak out about a bit of stress here or there even late in the day! The stress management tools discussed elsewhere in this chapter will assist in helping you navigate those events.

If, however, your cortisol undergoes stress-induced peaks in the late evening or nighttime, or if your morning cortisol is too low or declines too slowly, that flattening of the cortisol curve is what puts you into a state of chronic stress. [^115] This can cause a cascade of detrimental events in your body and brain. Diabetes, hypertension, depression, and weight gain can result, as can physical imbalance, leaving a person feeling unsteady on their feet. [^116] Studies have also linked abnormally high cortisol levels later in the day and into the night to acne, irregular menstrual cycles, and digestion issues. [^117] High cortisol at night has been linked to insomnia and reduced amounts of REM sleep. [^118] Given this, everyone would do well to try to anchor and amplify their cortisol and catecholamine peak in the first hours after waking to start their day and limit their cortisol and catecholamine levels at night. That simple framework goes a long way toward limiting your chronic stress. And that’s what this protocol is all about.

Let’s start with what to do at night, because how you prepare for bed affects your cortisol and catecholamine levels the next day. Some of what you’re about to read will be familiar to you from chapter 1. Before bed, implement a wind-down routine of dimming the lights, maybe taking a hot shower or bath or even washing your face with hot water. If you’re feeling stressed from the day, take a few moments to do some physiological sighs to lower your heart rate, and/or do a ten- to thirty-minute NSDR session. Don’t drink too many fluids or eat in the two to three hours before sleep, and definitely try to avoid caffeine in the eight to ten hours prior to bedtime. Viewing bright overhead LED lights (of the sort that are in many bathrooms) is a quick way to spike your cortisol and quash your melatonin, and checking your email or the news in the last hour before sleep is definitely a risky move if you want to keep your cortisol low at night (see chapter 1 for details). And to be clear: Low cortisol at night should be your goal!

If you happen to wake up in the middle of the night for whatever reason, avoid viewing bright lights or looking at your phone. Again, do some physiological sighs to help keep your heart rate low, and let yourself drift back to sleep. If you can’t fall back asleep, listen to an NSDR session. Or try the weird eye-movement trick I shared in chapter 1.

By the way, if you exercise in the evening or at night, that does significantly increase late-day cortisol. It’s better to exercise than not to, if you have a workout planned. To help keep your cortisol and catecholamine rhythms on a diurnal schedule, you can reduce the intensity of your evening training a bit and/or be sure to include a wind-down routine afterward. Andy Galpin, an exercise physiologist, encourages this after all workouts, but especially nighttime ones. Even moderate-intensity exercise can cause a large increase in cortisol (as discussed in chapter 2), especially if you consume caffeine first. [^119] That is one more reason to drink caffeine before moderate to intense exercise in the morning, but also to avoid it before moderate to intense exercise at night.

I don’t want to demonize late-day exercise. Better to do it than not do it. But just know that if you exercise intensely within four to six hours of bedtime, your next-day waking cortisol may be lower due to the negative feedback regulation of cortisol. [^120] That’s a mechanism you often see with hormones in the body, like cortisol or testosterone: When those hormones reach a certain high level, it signals specific brain areas and glands, such as the hypothalamus and pituitary and adrenals, to reduce their release of those hormones. Just another reason why spiking your morning cortisol is a good thing. It not only sets you up for the day, it helps keep cortisol levels low at night. [^121] So if you exercise at night and wonder why you’re dragging a bit the next morning, this may very well be why. Be diligent about using the tools in this protocol and you’ll be A-OK.

What about spiking your cortisol and catecholamines in the morning—how best to do that? There too you have options: Viewing bright light can boost your morning cortisol peak by 50 percent, making it a very easy, effective and beneficial practice (see Sleep Protocol 1 for more). Sunlight is ideal, but a 10,000 lux light works too. [^122] Hydration, caffeine, moderate to intense exercise, deliberate cold exposure, maybe cyclic hyperventilation (but never with deliberate cold exposure): Doing one of these is better than none, two is better than one, and so on. If I had to place them in order of effectiveness, I would say: sunlight viewing, exercise, and caffeine are the big levers here, but don’t worry about the order. Let logic be your guide. Obviously hydrate before and during your exercise, drink caffeine for an energy boost, get the sunlight before or during exercise if you can, but if the sun isn’t up and you’re ready to train, train! Don’t wait for the sun to rise, thinking that it has to come first because it’s a big lever. The cortisol and catecholamine systems are primed for release in the early hours of your day and will synergize without the need to get the relative timing (of all the things that cause their release) perfect.

When people ask me, “Who has time for all this?” I respond that it takes mere seconds to drink 16 ounces of water, a few minutes to make a caffeinated beverage and step outside into the sun while you drink it, and then depending on your schedule, exercise. Do not obsess over the details of relative timing of these tools.
A number of people have asked me over the years: “Given the importance of ensuring elevated morning cortisol, is there anything I can take to boost it besides caffeine?”

In chapter 6, I cover the many prescription drugs and supplements that can increase dopamine and norepinephrine, but when it comes to things that boost cortisol there are two that are particularly useful. And they are inexpensive. And commonplace. You may even have one of them in your kitchen right now.
They are grapefruit and licorice root extract. Not licorice candy, but licorice plant root extract. [^123]

Each can increase the size and duration of your morning cortisol peak and thereby increase your level of alertness and the other subjective effects associated with elevated sympathetic tone. How is this possible? Well…

Grapefruit impacts cortisol levels by two known mechanisms. First, it inhibits the enzyme (11β-HSD2) that blocks cortisol to cortisone conversion—cortisol being the chemical that imparts the functions we’ve been talking about so far in this protocol. Slower conversion means more active cortisol stays in our system for longer to impart its effects. Second, grapefruit inhibits the enzyme CYP3A4, which blocks the liver’s metabolism of cortisol, the net effect of which is to increase cortisol’s duration of action.
Licorice root extract contains something called glycyrrhizin (pronounced gly-cer-ry-zin) that potently inhibits the same abovementioned enzyme 11β-HSD2.

You may be thinking, Grapefruit and licorice?! Is he serious?! Yes, quite serious. There are human data to support the use of each to increase cortisol’s duration of action including studies demonstrating dose-dependent effects. So much so that well-informed MDs will warn patients with Cushing’s syndrome—which is a condition marked by pathologically elevated levels of cortisol—to avoid grapefruit, licorice root extracts, teas containing glycyrrhizin, and any licorice candy. (Note: Some traditional black licorice root candy, typically sold in Scandinavian countries but elsewhere too, contains glycyrrhizin, though versions without glycyrrhizin exist too.) I suggest most everyone avoid licorice root extract consumption late in the day and at night. If you want to experiment with taking licorice root extract that contains glycyrrhizin please talk to your doctor first. At high doses it can raise blood pressure, cause fluid retention, and even affect the metabolism of certain pharmaceutical drugs and potassium because of the many roles of the abovementioned enzymes in the liver.

I use licorice root extract with glycyrrhizin as a tool occasionally (once or twice a month). I find that 100 to 250 milligrams of licorice root in capsule form is enough to feel its effects. I make sure to use a version containing glycyrrhizin, and I take it with my morning caffeine usually before a hard workout that I need to start earlier than is typical for me. The energy-increasing effect is very noticeable. On very rare occasions I will take it around noon to try to extend my window of elevated cortisol to work for an especially long day, or to exercise hard midday. Again, I use it as a sometimes tool, not a regular tool, to boost cortisol in the morning.

Overall, grapefruit and grapefruit juice have a milder, but still meaningful, impact on cortisol’s duration of action. Most people can consume these without an adverse effect. But they can interact with various medications, so be sure to consult your doctor before taking. If you’d like to try incorporating grapefruit as a cortisol-boosting tool in your routine, perhaps eat a grapefruit or drink a small glass of grapefruit juice in the morning (pink or conventional is fine; it doesn’t matter). See how that affects your energy throughout the day. I would avoid these at night for obvious reasons.

One more thing to note here is that it is hard to find very-low-dose licorice root extract with glycyrrhizin. Most are 400 milligrams or more, and even at 200 milligrams it works very well to increase energy, so I empty half a 400 milligrams capsule into water or my coffee, and drink that. It tastes good. Remember: It raises blood pressure, and taking glycyrrhizin every day can lead to serious problems over time, so if you experiment with it, try a low dose—even if it means having to open up a capsule to remove a portion of the contents. Once more, talk to your doctor before you do. And if you have high blood pressure, don’t take it!

I can’t end this protocol without one more reminder about caffeine: If you consume caffeine in the late afternoon, too, don’t overdo it. I get it; I love yerba maté in the morning, and I love, love, love the taste of coffee in the afternoon. But if you’re an afternoon caffeine drinker and having sleep issues or trouble getting going in the mornings, you can bet it’s at least partially because the caffeine levels in your bloodstream are still too high from your afternoon coffee or tea. Try to drink only decaf after 2:00 p.m., or limit yourself to roughly 60 milligrams of caffeine (that’s about 3 to 4 ounces of regular coffee, or an espresso shot), and do your best to avoid it altogether within eight hours of bed (refer to Sleep Protocol 11 for more guidance). You could also opt to ditch the afternoon caffeine and instead to take 300 to 900 milligrams of alpha-GPC, which is a short-acting stimulant that can increase energy and focus and may actually improve REM sleep at night if taken six to ten hours before bedtime. I discuss this tool more in chapter 6.

This protocol includes several tools, so to recap: By increasing the slope and height of your morning cortisol and catecholamine peak, you buffer yourself against later-day stress in several ways. First, you’re likely to experience improved energy and focus for many hours afterward. Viewing bright light, [^124] consuming caffeine, [^125] exercise, [^126] and cold exposure [^127] all increase cortisol and/or catecholamine release. This helps us keep our reactions proportional to any stressors we may encounter later. By starting your day in a state of focus and readiness, if a stressful situation arises you don’t need to produce more cortisol to confront it effectively. Researchers who have examined the link between morning cortisol and stress call this connection the CAR anticipation hypothesis. [^128] It suggests that a big cortisol peak in the morning isn’t just to wake us up; it also prepares us for whatever stressors lie ahead. [^129]

And just remember this: You want your cortisol and catecholamines relatively high in the morning and daytime, and you want them low in the evening and at night. Stack the tools described here to do just that.
STRESS CONTROL PROTOCOL 6 Consider Specific Supplements to Help Offset Excessive Stress
WHAT TO DO

• Find a combination of supplements that might help you combat severe or prolonged periods of stress. Remember: Behavioral protocols are the foundation of mental and physical health and performance, and that is especially true when it comes to stress control. It’s also true that if your sleep duration and quality are not sufficient, no amount of pharmacology will help, at least not for long. Refer to chapter 1 for more on that topic. With that said, below is a list of supplements that have shown some efficacy for reducing various aspects of the stress response: Ashwagandha: 200–300 mg, 1 to 2 times per 24 hours, but taken only in the afternoon and/or evening.
• L-theanine: 100 mg or 200 mg, 1 to 3 times per day; if you drink caffeine regularly or are in a period of unusually high stress, take theanine with your caffeine.
• Phosphatidylserine: 400–800 mg, once per day anytime after 4:00 p.m.
• Rhodiola rosea: 200 mg, once or twice per day

• Proceed with caution. As always when discussing supplements or medication, it is important to consult with a physician. You need to be sure that you are not risking a dangerous interaction, that the product is reliable, and that a medical professional has information about what may be symptoms of an underlying health issue.
HOW IT WORKS

Certain supplements can help in times of excessive stress, such as when you are dealing with two or three nights of poor sleep due to an emotionally challenging circumstance, or if you’ve made behavioral changes but are still finding it hard to balance that autonomic seesaw. Alternatively, changes that occur with age can cause hormone surges or other shifts that can make you more vulnerable to stress.

On these occasions, certain supplements, taken alone or in combination, can help. The supplements in this protocol can increase parasympathetic nervous system activation and reduce sympathetic nervous system activation, either directly or indirectly, helping you to tilt that seesaw in the direction that is most beneficial to you. The studies described below are selected from the body of research on each supplement. These summaries are not comprehensive but provide an overview of the evidence.

If you decide to explore supplements for limiting stress, I would suggest taking one of them and seeing how it works for you before adding another. That is going to be the most informative and cost-effective approach. (I am well aware that some people will opt to just dive in and take all four because they hate stress that much. Try to hold back.)
Ashwagandha

Ashwagandha, also known as Indian ginseng or winter cherry, is used as an adaptogen—a term that broadly refers to substances that improve a person’s resistance to stress. A large review published in 2021 that included forty-one total studies in humans included seven that focused on stress and anxiety, enrolling a total of 491 adults who either reported being under high stress or were diagnosed with an anxiety disorder. [^130] Ashwagandha dosages varied from 240 milligrams per day to 1,250 milligrams per day for an extract and up to 6,000 milligrams when administered as a powdered root. (Most ashwagandha capsules sold over the counter in the US contain 200–600 mg per capsule.) Taken together, these studies showed that ashwagandha reduced stress and anxiety when compared to a placebo, and also reduced sleeplessness and fatigue. Cortisol levels in the blood were also lower among people taking this supplement, and it appeared that the cortisol-lowering effect of ashwagandha is likely the major basis of its effect on lowering stress and anxiety. A study of sixty adults found that those who took 225 milligrams or 400 milligrams per day of ashwagandha reported reductions in anxiety, depression, and food cravings compared to people randomized to a placebo. [^131] One study found that men and women taking ashwagandha had a 22 percent and 25 percent reduction in cortisol, respectively, when they took ashwagandha for sixty days versus taking a placebo for sixty days. [^132]

Research has identified several components that could contribute to the stress-reducing effects of ashwagandha. Most likely the effect is due to a “cocktail” of several different compounds in ashwagandha that work in parallel on various aspects of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, which, as you may remember from Sleep Protocol 1, is our main biological circuitry for mobilizing a physiological response to a stressor. The most potent of these mechanisms is the suppression of the signaling pathway for corticotropin (ACTH), a hormone that acts to stimulate the release of cortisol from your adrenals. [^133] The ashwagandha-suppression of corticotropin (ACTH) happens through a multistep process that begins with compounds called withanolides (naturally occurring plant hormones). These compounds can lower corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) in the hypothalamus. [^134] Limiting the amount of CRH in turn dampens the signaling that would normally trigger the release of cortisol. The fact that ashwagandha works “upstream” from the adrenal glands has a potential downside: Namely, it is likely to impact all the biology connected to CRH, which includes the gut and the immune system, among others. That’s one of several reasons why I suggest not taking ashwagandha at dosages higher than 600 milligrams per day for more than a few weeks before taking at least a few weeks off. There is at least one report of someone taking a high dose (950 mg) of ashwagandha daily for a year and developing adrenal insufficiency. [^135] People seem to vary quite a bit in their sensitivity to ashwagandha, so if you decide to try it in times of excess stress, I suggest starting with one dose per day, taken in the evening or an hour before bedtime at a dose of about 100 to 200 milligrams, and only increase the dosage, if needed, to find the minimal effective dose for you. Importantly, you don’t want to suppress cortisol in the early part of your day. If you decide to take more, take ashwagandha in the afternoon around 3:00 to 4:00 p.m., and perhaps again an hour before bedtime in a dosage of 200 to 300 milligrams each.

As mentioned above, I suggest you do not take ashwagandha at doses exceeding 600 milligrams per day for periods of longer than a couple of weeks. While the reports are largely anecdotal, some people taking high doses of ashwagandha (700–1,200 mg) per day experience apathy, starting about three to four weeks after continuous intake. The reasons for this are not clear and may be similar to the case report mentioned above, but because efficacy has been shown at lower doses of 300 to 600 milligrams per day, I suggest people use it as a tool to augment stress reduction by taking about 300 milligrams on a regular basis as described above, or reserve its use to high-stress periods and take higher dosages (greater than 600 mg/day) only during those times. And don’t let up on the behavioral practices for stress reduction.

A quick note about sourcing ashwagandha and other herbal adaptogens: The herbal supplement world is full of fake and contaminated products, perhaps even more so than for other types of supplements. Stick to major brands with third-party testing, especially ones that test for and remove metals from their products and ensure purity. Gaia Herbs has a good reputation for doing this and sells single-ingredient formulations. Barlow Herbals is another. I have no affiliation to either.
L-theanine

L-theanine is an amino acid present in green tea and has been recognized as one of its active compounds, alongside caffeine, catechins, and other molecules. [^136] Many studies of green tea have investigated a potential protective benefit against cancer and other chronic diseases, [^137] with the evidence from laboratory and animal studies indicating that it may reduce the risk of obesity and type 2 diabetes, as well as heart disease [^138] and breast cancer. [^139]

Large-scale clinical trials exploring the efficacy of theanine in humans are still lacking. It’s unlikely such studies will ever happen given their high cost and the fact that theanine is unlikely to be made into a pharmaceutical drug. That’s just how it goes with most naturally occurring compounds.

The reason L-theanine is in this chapter is that it is widely used to reduce arousal. That’s why nowadays L-theanine is sometimes added to energy drinks, and even to some coffee blends, to offset the jitters associated with drinking too much caffeine—presumably a clever trick on the part of the manufacturers that allows people to drink more of these beverages without feeling too strung out.

In one small, blinded, randomized study, thirty participants between the ages of thirty-six and sixty took L-theanine 200 milligrams per day or a placebo for four weeks. [^140] The investigators, a team from Japan, used several standard measures to gauge depression, anxiety, and sleep quality. They reported that the group taking L-theanine had significantly fewer stress-related symptoms.

In another study, a group of researchers in Australia and the Netherlands enrolled thirty-four adults between the ages of eighteen and forty in a blinded study to measure stress response in reaction to a series of cognitive tests involving mental arithmetic, memory, and coordination. [^141] Tasks like these can trigger stress because they challenge us. The tasks were presented following consumption of either a placebo or L-theanine as a nutrient drink. They found that the stress response, measured through the amount of salivary cortisol, was reduced compared to the placebo, an effect that appeared to last for several hours. In addition, the L-theanine group showed an increase in alpha brain waves, suggesting a more relaxed state of mind. That being said, cognitive performance was no different between the L-theanine and placebo groups. The reduced stress reaction may be beneficial for other reasons, but it’s useful to know that theanine didn’t make people better at the tasks they were given.
In terms of the underlying mechanisms, L-theanine research has found that this compound indirectly increases GABA—the major inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain—and dopamine. [^142]

Theanine taken in the hour before bedtime is part of the sleep stack I describe in chapter 1. There, I warned that people who have especially vivid dreams not take theanine. I suggest that people who want to try theanine to reduce their stress do so by taking about 200 milligrams of it in the early afternoon and perhaps another 100 to 200 milligrams again in the evening, especially if you had caffeine in the early afternoon.
Phosphatidylserine

Phosphatidylserine is a type of phospholipid. It is naturally found in the membranes of neurons, and comprises about 10 to 20 percent of the total phospholipid content of the brain—an enormous percentage when one considers that much of the nonliquid content of the brain is phospholipids. Naturally occurring phosphatidylserine plays a role in cognitive function, [^143] and the loss of phosphatidylserine in neurons known to occur in later adulthood may partially explain age-related (non-dementia) cognitive decline.

What’s more, in its natural state in our brains, this compound is known to decrease the stress response. [^144] As a supplement, phosphatidylserine has shown some benefit in older adults who experience chronic stress. There is some evidence phosphatidylserine taken late in the day may preferentially reduce evening and nighttime cortisol, [^145] which may explain how it indirectly supports sleep.

In one investigation, from 2004, participants took a phosphatidylserine supplement at a dose of 400 milligrams, 600 milligrams, or 800 milligrams, or a placebo (twenty people per group) and then completed a type of social stress test that involves performing in front of an audience. [^146] Data collected on biological indicators of the stress response revealed a significant decrease in these symptoms among the 400-milligram group, but not among those taking the higher doses (or the placebo). It’s hard to interpret the effect of higher doses, but this is not uncommon in pharmacology studies. Many studies of stress and cognitive performance show an inverted U-shaped response, where low- and high-dose conditions yield similar or no effects, but mid-range dosages do. Such are the complexities of biology. Another study found no link between phosphatidylserine and measures of a stress response across all sixty participants, but the researchers did observe an effect among participants with high chronic stress levels. [^147] Initially, this group had a diminished cortisol rise in response to a social stress test. That may sound like a good thing but it’s not. A blunted cortisol response is often a sign of underlying issues, such as depression. [^148] Treatment with phosphatidylserine appeared to restore the healthy rise in cortisol in response to the test, meaning it seemed to recalibrate the stress response rather than stop it. I say all this not to confuse you but to remind you that though the best model for your autonomic nervous system might be a seesaw, we need to consider the “hinge” of that seesaw (metaphorically speaking). How it bends, or sticks, matters. And compounds like phosphatidylserine may change people’s stress response by adjusting mechanisms analogous to how you might treat a hinge, rather than merely increasing or decreasing cortisol or adrenaline. Finally, in a six-week study from 2014 of seventy-five men randomized to phosphatidylserine (at a dose of 200 or 400 mg per day) or a placebo, the higher dose of the supplement appeared to lower the stress response among participants with chronic high stress. [^149]

If you opt to try phosphatidylserine for stress control, I recommend starting with a low dose of 100 to 200 milligrams, taken a few hours before bedtime, and increasing the dose only as needed. I know many people who like its effects on lowering stress late in the day, and for sleep.
Rhodiola rosea

Rhodiola rosea is a yellow-flowered plant that grows in northern regions of Europe and Asia and on the Atlantic coast of North America. It’s long been part of traditional medicine practices in Europe and Asia, used to address fatigue, mild anxiety, and symptoms of burnout. [^150] It is considered an adaptogen, because it alters the subjective experience of effort, apparently by adjusting the threshold for perceived effort, and by increasing effort endurance in physical and mental exertion. Subjectively, people taking Rhodiola rosea report less post-physical-exertion-related fatigue and that mental stressors feel less stressful, meaning they can lean into sustained effort without feeling exhausted. Indeed, Rhodiola rosea has been shown to reduce the symptoms of burnout, which is a multidimensional feature of chronic stress that includes the “wired but tired” feeling that is a common consequence of prolonged periods (days, weeks, etc.) of stress and altered sleep-wake cycles. European medical authorities approved the use of Rhodiola rosea for short-term relief of stress in 2012 [^151] and data on this connection have been slowly accruing.

One study examined the effects of Rhodiola rosea among fifty-six physicians working night shifts for fourteen days. [^152] Signs of mental fatigue were tested before and after the night shift for three two-week stretches. The investigators reported an improvement in tests examining memory, concentration, perception, and other aspects of brain function during the first two-week administration of Rhodiola rosea.

Another trial, from Russia, randomized 161 military cadets to one dose of Rhodiola rosea per day at either 370 milligrams or 555 milligrams, or placebo, and found a reduction in fatigue among both supplement groups. [^153] And in another investigation, a phase 3 clinical trial at Uppsala University, in Sweden, sixty people were randomized to receive four daily doses of Rhodiola rosea, for a total of 576 milligrams per day, or four placebo tablets. [^154] The participants completed several questionnaires gauging quality of life, depression, fatigue, and attention. Both groups experienced improvements in overall mental health and reduced feelings of burnout. But in the group taking Rhodiola rosea, the reduction in fatigue was more pronounced, and linked to improvements in performance and concentration.

Rhodiola rosea is among the better-studied supplements for stress control, and we have copious evidence pointing to its usefulness in this context. With regard to the underlying mechanism, Rhodiola rosea contains numerous phytochemicals (compounds made by plants) that could contribute to its benefits, including by interacting with cortisol pathways [^155] and by activating heat-shock proteins, [^156] which our cells make in response to stressful conditions such as the excessive heat or cold, the presence of heavy metals, or an infection. Researchers are still investigating the exact mechanisms tied to the stress-reducing effects, as well as its apparent contribution to physical strength and endurance. [^157] The picture emerging is that Rhodiola rosea buffers against stress by calibrating the amount of adrenaline that is released in moments of high physical exertion and high emotional stress.

I recommend one of two approaches to trying Rhodiola rosea. The first is to take it thirty to sixty minutes before a known stressor, like a hard workout or big exam or study session or public speaking engagement—basically any event that you know will require an intense and prolonged effort. I take 120 to 240 milligrams of Rhodiola rosea before hard resistance training workouts, which is per the standard protocol used in most peer-reviewed studies of Rhodiola rosea for physical exertion. The second way to take Rhodiola rosea is during periods of chronic stress, when you can’t get as much sleep as you would like and/or when your output is greater than usual. Think final exam week, the days of long work hours before a vacation, the vacation with your in-laws where you are coordinating everything, et cetera. In those times, I suggest taking 100 to 120 milligrams (the typical capsule dose of Rhodiola rosea in most supplements) three times daily (morning, afternoon, and evening). It can be taken with or without food. I would not suggest taking Rhodiola rosea multiple times throughout the day for more than three to four weeks without taking a break of at least two weeks, as all the biological pathways Rhodiola rosea is known to impact are subject to feedback loops and downregulation. Use 100-milligrams-plus daily dosages of Rhodiola rosea as a short-term tool to combat stress and burnout, not as a mainstay of your supplement regimen. And I know I sound like a broken record, but don’t just pile on supplements for managing stress. You need—and now have—multiple behavioral tools to reduce stress. Use them!
